text: Sydney Shoemaker explains the special authority of first-person, present-tense psychological avowals (such as 'I am in pain') by:
choices: showing that such avowals are strictly infallible and incorrigible, exactly as Descartes maintained
treating them as high-level perceptual reports produced by an inner-sense faculty scanning one's own mental representations
noting that they are not based on observation of evidence, are not reached by inference, and are not subject to error through misidentification of whose state it is
reducing first-person authority to the same inductive track record that grounds ordinary third-person attributions
explanation: Shoemaker grounds first-person authority not in infallibility but in the absence of certain error-possibilities: avowals are not evidence-based, not inferential, and immune to error through misidentification (one does not wonder whether it is oneself who is in pain), yielding a distinctive but still defeasible authority. Option 0 is the stronger Cartesian infallibility Shoemaker avoids; option 1 is Carruthers' inner-sense model; option 3 collapses the very first/third-person asymmetry being explained. Only option 2 is Shoemaker's account.
